newsitem.title: USA: Budget expected to pass over Gephardt opposition.
newsitem.headline: Budget expected to pass over Gephardt opposition.

text.p: White House officials said Tuesday they were confident a hard-won agreement to balance the budget by 2002 will pass Congress quickly despite opposition of the top Democrat in the House.

House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, a potential contender for the Democratic Party's presidential nomination in 2000, announced he will vote against the budget on the grounds that it cuts too deeply into Medicare health care programmes for the elderly while giving the wealthy a tax break.
In remarks prepared for delivery before the House, Gephardt said, "I refuse to be a party to an agreement that balances the budget in name only."

Despite Gephardt's urging of his colleagues to defeat the plan, President Clinton's budget director Franklin Raines said he expected the measure to pass the House and Senate. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Gephardt's decision would not have any bearing on future work with this key Democrat.

"He (Gephardt) is a very highly valued member of the Democratic team on the Hill and the President has great affection, admiration and respect for him and will continue to work with him," McCurry said.

The House votes late in the day while the Senate was scheduled to open debate on amendments. Leaders of both chambers expect the measure will pass. But before that point is reached, many lawmakers will seek to change the budget or to offer alternatives.
"We will achieve our goal of having a majority of Democrats supporting the (budget) resolution," Raines told reporters after listening to Gephardt's arguments at a closed meeting of House Democrats.
The budget slows the growth of government spending for the next five years, cuts Medicare by $115 billion and brings the deficit from this year's forecasted $67 billion to zero by 2002.

It also provides a net $85 billion tax cut which Raines said they had assurances from Republican leaders would largely benefit families with children and those who have students seeking post-secondary education.

But Gephardt said Republicans had forced acceptance of the tax cut in return for support for a balanced budget. "They should not use the ruse of balancing the budget to cover their real intent," he said

"At a time when we are asking average, hard-working Americans to tighten their belts, we shouldn't be telling the wealthiest Americans that, not only don't they have to participate, they'll actually get a huge tax cut."

Under the Republican tax proposals which will be before the tax-writing committees, Gephardt said the wealthiest one percent will see their taxes reduced by $6,784 a year. This group earns an average of $645,000 a year.
And, he argued that the the tax cuts will cause the deficit to explode after 2002.

The tax cut of $85 billion is a small fraction of the nearly $10 trillion in taxes to be collected by the government by individuals and businesses over the next five years. At the same time, the government will spend $1.6 trillion in fiscal 1997, rising to $1.9 trillion in fiscal 2002.

Congressional budget committees said that over its five years the plan cuts $304 billion in spending from what would have occurred without changes in policy, but it gives Clinton $33 billion to spend on education, the environment and his other important domestic goals.
According to the congressional budget panels, this budget deal would result in an increase in the deficit next year to $90 billion from an expected $67 billion in current fiscal 1997.

The deficit would start to decline in two years and would hit a slight surplus of $1 billion in 2002. Based on the estimates of economic growth and tax revenues, the budget would show a surplus of $34 billion by 2007.
